subject: Maths
title: Double inequalities
subtitle: Linear Inequalities · GCSE Maths
learning_objective: I can solve and represent double (compound) inequalities.

key_vocab.definition: A double inequality has the variable between two bounds, e.g. 3 greater than 3 AND less than or equal to 7 simultaneously.

sections.title: Learning Objective
sections.content: I can solve and represent double (compound) inequalities.

sections.title: Key Words
sections.content: double inequality -- A double inequality has the variable between two bounds, e.g. 3 greater than 3 AND less than or equal to 7 simultaneously.

sections.title: Method
sections.content:
Whatever you do to the middle, do the same to the left and right. If you multiply/divide by a negative, reverse both inequality signs.
a bx + c ≤ d ⇒ &frac{a − c}{b} x ≤ &frac{d − c}{b}
Subtract c, then divide by b (all three parts)

Key examples:
  ✓ 2 < x ≤ 5 means x can be 3, 4, or 5 (integers)  (inclusive of 5)
  ✓ −1 ≤ x < 4 includes −1 but not 4  (closed/open)
  ✓ 1 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9 gives 0 < x ≤ 4  (solve all three parts)
  ✗ 2 < x ≤ 5 means x can be 2  (strict inequality excludes 2)
  ✗ To solve, only work on the middle part  (must do same to all three parts)

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Example 1 – listing integers
  List the integers satisfying −2 < x ≤ 3
  x must be greater than −2 (not including −2)
  x must be less than or equal to 3
  Integers: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3
  −1, 0, 1, 2, 3
  (Open circle at −2 (not included), closed at 3 (included).)

Example 2 – solving a double inequality
  Solve 4 < 2x + 2 ≤ 10
  Subtract 2 from all parts: 2 < 2x ≤ 8
  Divide all parts by 2: 1 < x ≤ 4
  Solution: 1 < x ≤ 4
  1 < x ≤ 4
  (Perform identical operations on all three parts.)

sections.title: Listing integers
sections.content:
List all integers satisfying each inequality.

(a) 1 < x ≤ 5
(b) −3 ≤ x < 2
(c) 0 < x < 4
(d) −1 ≤ x ≤ 3

sections.title: Solving (add/subtract)
sections.content:
Solve each double inequality.

(a) 3 < x + 1 ≤ 7
(b) 1 ≤ x − 2 < 5
(c) −4 < x + 3 ≤ 6
(d) 0 ≤ x − 5 < 3

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
✓ 2 < x ≤ 5 means x can be 3, 4, or 5 (integers)
✗ 2 < x ≤ 5 includes 2
✓ Dividing by a negative reverses both inequality signs
✗ You only need to solve the right-hand inequality
✓ A double inequality can be split into two separate inequalities

teacher_sections.content:
Award marks for correct working and final answers.

Listing integers:
  (a) 2, 3, 4, 5
  (b) −3, −2, −1, 0, 1
  (c) 1, 2, 3
  (d) −1, 0, 1, 2, 3

Solving (add/subtract):
  (a) 2 < x ≤ 6
  (b) 3 ≤ x < 7
  (c) −7 < x ≤ 3
  (d) 5 ≤ x < 8

Solving (multiply/divide):
  (a) 2 < x ≤ 5
  (b) 2 ≤ x < 5
  (c) 4 < x ≤ 10
  (d) &frac{1}{4} < x ≤ 5

Two-step solving:
  (a) 2 < x ≤ 5; integers 3, 4, 5
  (b) 1 ≤ x < 4; integers 1, 2, 3
  (c) −2 < x ≤ 3; integers −1, 0, 1, 2, 3
  (d) 1 ≤ x < 4; integers 1, 2, 3

Mixed and harder:
  (a) −3 < x ≤ 2
  (b) 2 < x ≤ 5
  (c) −4 ≤ x < 4
  (d) −1 < x ≤ 5
  (e) −2 ≤ x < 5
